Rencontre avec Norman Ajari, docteur en: A conversation with Norman Ajari, PhD in philosophy and lecturer in Francophone Black studies, about decolonial philosophy.
Norman Ajari, docteur en philosophie et: Norman Ajari, PhD in philosophy and lecturer in Francophone Black studies at the University of Edinburgh. Photo: Aude Simon
Je suis contente de vous présenter Norma: I’m happy to introduce Norman Ajari for this first interview of Les Grandes Converses. He holds a PhD in philosophy and is a lecturer in Francophone Black studies at the University of Edinburgh, in Scotland. We talked about Afro-decolonial philosophy, but also about anti-Black racism.
Pour ma part, c'était la première fois q: For me, it was the first time I had met a Black philosopher. I remember, at 17, the philosophy classes in my school curriculum, which could either captivate me or bore me to sleep.
Je me dis que, peut-être, si on m'avait: I tell myself that maybe, if someone had told me about even one philosopher of African descent, everything would have been different! And that’s what I wanted to do for you here.
Le programme scolaire n’est pas toujours: The school curriculum isn’t always easy, and it’s even less so when you feel implicitly excluded. Still, I’m very happy for the next generations: representation is starting to appear, and it comes from accessible, cool people like Norman.
Lisez le texte, mais surtout regardez la: Read the text, but above all, watch the video! Norman is funny, sharp, and knows how to demystify subjects that can seem heavy.
<strong><em>Norman Ajari, docteur en phi: Norman Ajari, PhD in philosophy and lecturer in Francophone Black studies at the University of Edinburgh, in Scotland, is visiting Quebec for the second time. We met him at the La Converse offices, where he spoke candidly about decolonial philosophy and anti-Black racism.
Du haut de ses 2 mètres, vêtu d’une vest: Standing 2 metres tall, dressed in a sober suit jacket and dress shoes, Norman Ajari seems reserved at first glance. But as soon as he starts talking about philosophy, his humour and a great natural ease come through. Small pink cup of matcha in hand, the intellectual makes the most complex subjects feel light. Serious and funny at once, he manages to demystify philosophy and captivate his audience.
« Je vais essayer de parler en langage o: “I’ll try to speak in ordinary language, as they say,” the philosopher begins, bursting into laughter.
<strong>La Converse : Tu es un spécialis: La Converse: You’re a specialist in decolonization and Afro-decolonization. Can you explain the particularities of these liberation movements and how they differ?
La décolonisation, c’est toutes les entr: Decolonization is all the undertakings, all the political movements, all the activism that arose to get rid of the colonizers. If we’re talking about the 20<sup>th</sup> century, decolonization was the movement to reclaim political and economic autonomy and sovereignty over territories in Africa and large parts of Asia that had been conquered by European powers. It’s a long process, one that is still not completely finished and that, at times, is particularly unfinished.
La décolonisation a de plus en plus une: Decolonization increasingly has an intellectual dimension, a dimension where it is possible to develop your own thinking. Because thought has often been the preserve of the white world. The ideas of Black populations, Asian populations and Indigenous populations were discredited and were considered inferior, as lacking universal value and intrinsic quality.
La décolonisation peut donc avoir plusie: So decolonization can have several dimensions: economic and political, but it can also be a kind of intellectual liberation.
Une philosophie afro-décoloniale cherche: An Afro-decolonial philosophy seeks to carry out this project of decolonization in the service of, and through an understanding of, the Black experience.
La philosophie populaire est née de l’ém: Popular philosophy was born of wonder, of astonishment. From there, people began asking philosophical questions like: “What is beauty? What is kindness?” That’s what we find in Plato’s dialogues. In short, it’s good old-fashioned philosophy.
Mais le problème, c’est que, pour l’expé: But the problem is that, for the Black experience – as the Cameroonian philosopher Fabien Eboussi Boulaga explains – philosophy doesn’t begin with wonder or astonishment. It begins with the stupor caused by a total defeat. A stupor in the face of colonial dehumanization.
Aujourd’hui encore, être Noir, ça signif: Even today, being Black means being a descendant of enslaved or colonized people. All Black people descend from populations whose humanity was denied by all of Western science: philosophy, literature, law, economics, biology.
Bref, toutes les sciences occidentales s: In short, all of Western science came together – from the Enlightenment to the early 20<sup>th</sup> century – to say that Black people are inferior. So we live in a world that is historically oriented around a denial of Black peoples. Naturally, Black philosophy can’t start from the same point.
Donc, même si c’est douloureux, la philo: So, even if it’s painful, Afro-decolonial philosophy aims to reflect on all the consequences of the violence that Black people have suffered, to try to reclaim that humanity, to rebuild it and, above all, to try to produce some form of reparation.
<strong>Aujourd’hui, le Québec, tout com: Today, Quebec, like France, refuses to acknowledge the existence of systemic racism. Why, in your view?
Je pense que c’est tout simplement l’inf: I think it’s simply the French influence that plays a major role here. It’s not so much explicit racism as a legacy of French political philosophy, notably that of Rousseau, which promotes an abstract vision of the citizen: an individual who judges laws solely according to the general interest, without taking into account their class, gender, race or religion.
Bien sûr, ce modèle universaliste issu d: Of course, this universalist model that came out of the Enlightenment is philosophically, speculatively very beautiful. But in practice, it’s simply laws that protect the powerful by telling the poor and the oppressed not to consider their own interests, but rather those of society as a whole.
Les francophones, notamment au Québec, r: Francophones, especially in Quebec, remain seduced by the elegance of this philosophical tradition. Yet after centuries of labour, Marxist and anti-racist struggles, these ideas now seem outdated and ineffective. It’s a servile imitation of France, a desire to reproduce or even surpass its legacy. It results in a system that, under refined and subtle appearances, perpetuates social inequalities – it’s the quintessence of the worst that France can give the world.
<strong>Y a-t-il une grande différence d: Is there a big difference in how the concept of “race” is perceived in the Francophone world and the Anglophone world?
Il y a effectivement des sensibilités di: There are indeed different diplomatic sensibilities. On the Anglophone side, for example, putting forward your condition as a Black woman, making a personal narrative out of it, is great.
Pour les francophones, il faut être dans: For Francophones, you have to be in a universalist discourse, try to show that you’re part of a diversity, but a slightly more acceptable one. So if we’re in a kind of diplomacy, we can’t speak the same language to them. There are different political sensibilities, and we’re obliged, especially if we have to negotiate money, to speak a different language and adapt to different political imaginaries in order to be seen as legitimate.
Dans le contexte québécois, il ne faut s: In the Quebec context, you absolutely must not bring in discourses that crack national unity, especially if it’s to negotiate money.
Sur le plan universitaire également, tou: At the university level too, all the Francophone countries of the Global North have universities where Black studies are simply not developed. That’s obviously the opposite of what happens in the United States or in Britain, where I teach myself, or in English Canada. It hurts a bit, let’s put it that way. There’s no will to develop Black thought. Black people are still assigned to sports, to athletic performance – clichés that have a strong link to the history of slavery.
Mais dire qu’il y a une vraie différence: But to say there’s a real difference between the Anglophone and Francophone contexts in North America, or in Europe? I don’t believe that for a second.
<strong>Il y a cette idée populaire selo: There’s a popular idea that Francophones are more racist than Anglophones. Do you agree?
Non et ils se renvoient tout simplement: No, and they’re simply passing the buck back and forth. Francophones point to American prisons and say: “Look, they’re the real racists.” Anglophones, for their part, answer: “No, look at the Francophones instead, they don’t acknowledge systemic racism.”
En réalité, ils sont racistes de manière: In reality, they’re racist in different ways, that’s all. In Quebec, as in the United States, the clichés about Black people are identical. “Black people who love chicken, who have big lips, who are lazy...” They’re the same clichés because this continent was colonized by three major slaveholding powers: the Spanish, the French and the British. All these nations took part in the transatlantic slave trade, and their legacy of negrophobia is the same. There is no place where the image of Black people is better than elsewhere. The stereotypes about Black bodies, the sexualization of Black women or the fantasy around the Black man’s penis – all of that crosses cultures and languages.
<strong>Peut-on espérer se débarrasser u: Can we hope to one day get rid of the clichés and structures that perpetuate negrophobia?
Malheureusement, ce qui fige la négropho: Unfortunately, what locks negrophobia in place around the world is the overexploitation of and violence against Africa. We live in a world where the economic and political situation of vast parts of the African continent is still seen as proof of Black inferiority.
On peut toujours utiliser cet argument l: That argument can always be used when a Black person wants to get ahead: “But you Black people, you’re always inferior. Look at the situation in Africa: you’re not capable of governing yourselves, etc.”
Ainsi, le colonialisme, l’extractivisme: So colonialism, extractivism in Africa and coups d’état have, of course, the primary goal of securing the exploitation of resources by multinationals. But they also have a secondary function, conscious or not: to maintain and justify the inferiorization and exploitation of Black people, including here.
Mais évidemment, ça ne doit pas servir d: But obviously, that must not serve as an excuse for not fighting this more ordinary racism here. Because these are quite simply human rights.
<strong>Comment peut-on combattre ce rac: How can we fight this anti-Black racism, in your view?
Je crois fermement que l’organisation co: I firmly believe that collective organizing is the key. There are a lot of individuals suffering in their own corner, who don’t really know how to fight systemic racism because it’s sometimes pre-empted by the government.
Bien que les initiatives gouvernementale: While government initiatives like support programs for Black entrepreneurs are good, they’re not enough. The problem is that these are measures that tend to balkanize people a little: we bring these Black people together for training, but each of them has their own goal, their own project. These measures sometimes tend to individualize problems by emphasizing personal success rather than collective struggle.
Ce qui est fondamental, ce n’est même pa: What’s fundamental isn’t even to get politically involved or to create a political organization like the Black Panthers. It’s essential to pass on to younger generations the history of anti-racist struggles: to share the legacy of Black thought, of what our ancestors did – how they thought about society, about the obstacles Black people faced in society. Once that transmission begins, we have to encourage them to organize around projects they’re passionate about. It’s by taking ownership of their history and connecting with past struggles that young people will be effective in transforming society.
<strong>As-tu un conseil pour un jeune n: Do you have advice for a young Black person or a young racialized person who wants to become a philosopher?
Évidemment, lisez. Lisez des auteurs noi: Obviously, read. Read Black authors, be curious. Don’t hesitate to do like music diggers, to go underground, to look for Black thinkers from your countries of origin. Look at the history of neighbouring countries, the history of the diaspora, and let yourself get lost in it.
Une grande partie du militantisme noir e: A big part of Black activism is a matter of consciousness. It’s not very trendy anymore to be woke, but it’s knowledge. Moving through a world shaped by our knowledge of Black history means entering a process of self-transformation. Becoming rich isn’t the only project worth pursuing – acquiring wisdom, and all the more so Black wisdom, is a real project for the future.
